title: Ludwig van Beethoven's Life In Reverse | From a Währing Cemetery to a Bonn Baptism
description:
Beethoven's life runs backwards in this episode, opening with his death in Vienna in 1827 and rewinding to his baptism in Bonn in 1770. The journey steps through the symphony premiered to a packed hall in 1824, the siege of Vienna in 1809, the Heiligenstadt letter in which he told his brothers he could no longer hear, and the keyboard lessons his father arranged for a boy of seven. Every scene moves to an earlier year, so the music arrives in reverse order and the years of deafness behind it come into view. Dates, places and premieres follow the documented record, and the stories told later about him are reported as stories.

scenes.narration: The tune that fills the last movement of his ninth symphony was taken as an official anthem by the Council of Europe in 1972 and is now played at the ceremonies of the European Union. He set it to words written by a German poet half a century earlier, and the manuscript of the music is kept in a library in Berlin.

He died at home in Vienna on March 26, 1827, at the age of fifty-six, after a winter in which he could not leave his rooms. He had been ill since the previous autumn, and the illness was managed with treatments that did not work. He remained clear to the end and gave instructions about his papers.

Three days later he was carried through the streets of Vienna to the cemetery at Währing, and the crowd that followed was large enough to be talked about for years afterwards. Poets of the city wrote the words spoken over the grave, and musicians from the theatres walked behind the coffin with their bands playing.

Through his last winter he lay with the proof sheets of his latest string quartet on the blanket, marking corrections while visitors sat with him. He also set down sketches for another symphony that he did not finish. The quartet was already in the hands of the engraver, and he had promised it to a publisher in Berlin.

In 1826 he completed the last of the string quartets he had been writing since 1825, for players who read music closely and for rooms built for that size of sound. They were hard to follow for listeners used to his symphonies. He worked on them at his brother's house in the country and finished them after the trouble that summer.

In July 1826 his nephew, whom he had raised and fought a court to keep, shot himself in the house and survived. The wound and the scandal kept Beethoven indoors for weeks. He had taken the boy in after the death of his brother, and the arrangement had turned sour over money, work and the aunt's family.

The first of the late quartets was heard in Vienna in March 1825, written for a Russian nobleman who had asked him for quartets three years earlier. The audience was small and the players were specialists. Beethoven was fifty-four, deaf, and writing music that most of the city did not know what to do with.

On May 7, 1824, a new symphony with voices in its last movement was performed for the first time at the theatre on the Kärntnerstrasse in Vienna, together with three movements of a mass he had finished the year before. The singers had to turn him round so that he could see the applause, because he could not hear it. He stood among them while the room stood up.

He began the great mass in 1819 for the installation of his pupil and patron as archbishop, and the date passed before he could finish it, so he worked on it until 1823. The first complete performance was given in St Petersburg in April 1824 by a Russian nobleman who had bought a copy in advance. In Vienna the censors allowed three movements only, and only if they were billed as hymns.

From 1818 his hearing had gone so far that visitors wrote what they wanted to say in notebooks, and he answered out loud. Hundreds of these books survive, and in them the conversations of the last decade of his life are recorded in other people's handwriting. He kept composing through all of it, and the pieces went out to publishers in Berlin, Vienna and London.

In November 1815 his brother died in Vienna and left a wife and a son. Beethoven went to court to take the boy out of her hands, and the case ran for five years until he won guardianship in 1820. The boy was called Karl. The fight cost him fees, five years and the good will of people he had counted as friends.

In November 1814 he put his only opera on the stage for the fourth time, with the words rewritten and the music cut down, and at last the house was full. It had failed at its first performance in 1805 and again the year after. He never wrote another opera, and the piece kept coming back to him as a problem he had not settled.

In December 1813 he finished a piece built on a recent British victory over the French, using two tunes the audience already knew by heart. It was played again and again that month, it suited a Vienna full of soldiers and news from the war, and it brought him more money in one season than anything he had written before.

In the summer of 1812 he took the waters at a spa in Bohemia and there wrote a long private letter to a woman he called his immortal beloved, which he kept instead of sending. The addressee has never been established with certainty, and biographers have argued over her for two centuries. He went home by way of Prague.

In May 1809 the French army bombarded Vienna, and he sat out the shelling in the cellar of his brother's house with his hands pressed over his ears. An offer of a post came from a German court soon after, and three noblemen of Vienna agreed to pay him an annual sum on condition that he stayed where he was.

On December 22, 1808, two of his symphonies were heard for the first time at a long concert in Vienna that he arranged himself and that ran far into the night. Both had been finished that year, and a new piano concerto of his, which he played himself, stood between them on the programme. He was thirty-seven.

His opera was given for the first time in November 1805 at a theatre in Vienna, in the middle of an occupation, with the houses thin and half the audience made up of French officers. It had taken him years of work. Two more versions followed over the next few years before the piece found its shape.

In 1804 he finished a symphony on a scale that the players who read it found hard to sit through, having begun it the year before. He had first dedicated it to the French first consul, then scratched the dedication out when the news reached Vienna that the man had crowned himself emperor. His pupil later described how the title page was torn out of the fair copy.

On October 6, 1802, at Heiligenstadt outside Vienna, he wrote a letter to his two brothers telling them that his hearing was failing, that he had no hope of a cure, and that he had decided to keep going only for the sake of his work. He never gave it to them. It is the clearest statement he left of what the silence was costing him.

In 1801 he finished a sonata for the piano and dedicated it to a young countess he was in love with. The name it is known by was given by a writer years after his death, from a comparison of the first movement to moonlight on a lake. He himself called it a fantasia, and the name stuck anyway.

On April 2, 1800, his first symphony was played in Vienna at the court theatre in a program of his own, with an octet, two overtures and a piano concerto beside it. He was twenty-nine and had been in the city for eight years. The evening gave his name to listeners who until then had known him only as a pianist.

Through the later 1790s he travelled between the courts of the German lands as a pianist who could be relied on to fill a room. Prague, Dresden and Berlin were all on his route, and he played for princes, officers and paying subscribers in turn. He was still young enough to take the road, and the name he made abroad ran ahead of him back to Vienna.

His first benefit at the court theatre in Vienna came in March 1795, when he played a concerto of his own to a hall of subscribers who already knew him by reputation. He was twenty-four, from a town on the Rhine that had lost its court to the French, and he had come to stay. The money from the evening was his to keep.

He reached Vienna in November 1792 with letters of introduction to the court, and he began lessons with Joseph Haydn in the winter that followed. He found the teaching hurried and looked for another master, and he went on studying counterpoint for years with men who charged by the lesson. He also had to find lodgings, pupils and a publisher.

He had already left Bonn for good when his father, the court singer who had driven him at the keyboard as a child, was put out of his post for drinking and died in December 1792. The two sons had been earning for years and the household had leaned on them. The court that paid the family was itself within two years of disappearing.

In the summer of 1787 he went to Vienna for the first time to study, and later in life he said that he had played to Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. No letter of Mozart's mentions him, and the story rests on the accounts of people who heard it afterwards. Within weeks his mother was ill at home, and he travelled back to Bonn to sit with her until she died.

In 1784, at fourteen, he was put on the payroll of the electoral court at Bonn, playing the organ in the chapel and the viola in the theatre orchestra beside men twice his age. The court paid late and often in arrears. The household began to lean on the boy's income from that year on, and he kept the post for the rest of his time in the town.

In 1782 he printed his first piece, a set of variations on a march, issued by a bookseller on the Rhine. He was eleven. It came out while he was still at school in Bonn, and it told the region that the son of Johann van Beethoven could write as well as play.

As a small boy he was set at the keyboard for hours each day and taken out to be played on in the hope that a prodigy would bring money to a family that always needed it. His father sang in the chapel of the elector and drank. The boy went to the town school between the lessons, and his mother kept the house going around them.

He was born in December 1770 in Bonn, a town on the Rhine where the archbishop also ruled as an elector of the empire, and he was baptised the next day at the parish church. The family name was already known at court. Two brothers followed him, and the three of them grew up in the same narrow house.
